claims.text: Elevated oxygen partial pressure during sliding wear causes rapid oxide-layer formation on CoCrFeMnNi coatings.
The resulting oxide layer is adherent and nanocomposite.
The oxide layer acts as a lubricating barrier.
Formation of the oxide layer reduces wear relative to wear in an inert atmosphere.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi coatings are uniform and lack a pre-formed oxide layer.
Sliding-wear tests should compare an oxygen-enhanced atmosphere with an argon atmosphere while holding temperature, load, and sliding speed constant.
Frictional heating and mechanical agitation induce rapid tribo-oxidation in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
Tribo-oxidation produces a fine, adherent oxide film.
The oxide film reduces metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide film functions as a solid lubricant.
The proposed tribo-oxidation process is absent under inert conditions.
Argon testing prevents oxide-layer formation and consequently produces higher wear rates.
The proposed effect should hold at room temperature over normal loads and sliding speeds typical of wear-resistant applications.
The proposed effect requires an oxygen partial pressure sufficiently above the inert baseline.
The proposed effect will cease to be beneficial when oxygen exposure causes continuous bulk oxidation or degradation.
The oxygen partial-pressure threshold for reliable beneficial oxide formation is unknown.
Failure to form the oxide layer under elevated oxygen would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reduce wear under elevated oxygen would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says either similar wear rates or lack of oxide formation would falsify the hypothesis, whereas the formal falsification rule requires both lack of a consistent oxide layer and lack of wear reduction. These OR and AND criteria yield different decisions.
